findings.evidence: Table 7-2 caption: "Table 7-2 — Memory floors by regime: inference and fine-tuning variants for the canonical 80-layer, hidden-8192, full-MHA 70B reference model." Rows give ~164.1 GB, ~152 GB, ~1,120 GB, ~280 GB, ~36 GB with no provenance/epistemic labels in any row and no table-level label convention stated.
findings.issue: Evidence-label defect: Table 7-2 presents load-bearing quantitative values with no [canonical scenario]/[DERIVED]/[ASSUMPTION] labels. The Preface states a claim must carry labels inline or via an identified table/section that states them for every row; this table does neither, unlike Table 4-2 (Status column) and Table 7-1 (per-row labels).
findings.fix_instruction: Add a provenance/status column or a table-level label note to Table 7-2 (e.g. [canonical scenario][DERIVED] for the 70B arithmetic rows, [1P][FACT] for the FP16/IEEE constants), consistent with Table 7-1 and Table 4-2.

findings.evidence: Figure 7.5 caption: "FP16 bound reaches the 436 GB budget at ~166K" ... "the GQA FP16 line at 327,680 B/token reaches that budget only at ~1.33M tokens"
findings.issue: Figure-vs-text unit inconsistency: the figure's vertical axis is labeled "KV cache size (GB)" and the caption says "The axis and every series are aggregate whole-host GB". The 436 GB budget is an aggregate whole-host figure. But the 9.5K GQA annotation "≈ 3.1 GB (GQA FP16)" is a per-rank value (24.9 ÷ 8), not an aggregate whole-host value — the caption admits this ("24.9 ÷ 8 ≈ 3.1 GB per rank at 9.5K, to be read against an 80 GB rank, not against the aggregate budget line"). Mixing per-rank and aggregate values on one aggregate axis is confusing.
findings.fix_instruction: Move the per-rank 3.1 GB annotation off the aggregate axis, or relabel it explicitly as "per-rank" and draw it against a secondary per-rank axis; alternatively, plot the aggregate GQA value (~24.9 GB at 9.5K) on the aggregate axis.

findings.evidence: "The KV budget on a nominal 24 GB device is therefore 20 GB (24 − 4)."
findings.issue: Label 'KV budget' for 20 GB is misleading. The 20 GB (24 − 4 reserve) is the budget for weights + KV combined; after the 16 GB of weights are subtracted, only 4 GB remains available for KV. A reader may interpret 20 GB as space available for KV alone, which would be a 5× overestimate of actual KV headroom. The subsequent statement that the device passes (total 21.245 GB < 24 GB) is correct, but the label on the intermediate quantity is imprecise.
findings.fix_instruction: Rename to 'weights + KV budget after reserve' or 'model budget after reserve' (20 GB), or state the actual KV-available space: '24 − 4 − 16 = 4 GB available for KV.'

findings.evidence: Page 146: "Unit basis (locked): the H100's quoted 80 GB is treated as decimal 80×10^9 B throughout, so the canonical 8×H100 pool reads 640 GB. The vendor-binary reading is 81,559 MiB ≈ 85.5×10^9 B per part ... which would give 2×H100 = 171.0 GB and an ~684 GB host pool. One conversion rule covers every capacity-dependent figure below: on that basis the KV budget becomes ~480 GB (684 − 140 − 64) and the per-host concurrency ceiling ~19 (480 ÷ 24.9037 = 19.3; floor 19), against 436 GB and ~17.5 (floor 17) on the decimal basis."
findings.issue: Recompute: 81,559 MiB × 1,048,576 B/MiB = 85,499,536,384 B ≈ 85.5×10^9 ✓; 2 × 85.5 = 171.0 ✓; 8 × 85.5 = 684 ✓; 684 − 140 − 64 = 480 ✓; 480 ÷ 24.9037 = 19.27 → floor 19 ✓. The arithmetic is correct and the convention is explicitly locked — good practice. The defect is that the unit-basis paragraph is placed inside §7.1 ('Unit basis (locked)') but it quantifies the KV budget and concurrency ceiling, which are §7.3's results (Table 7-1, Fig 7.7). A reader in §7.1 encounters ~436 GB, ~17.5, ~480 GB and ~19 — the chapter's headline numbers — before the arithmetic that produces them (Table 7-1) has been presented.
findings.fix_instruction: Move the alternate-basis recomputation of the KV budget and concurrency ceiling to §7.3 (immediately after Table 7-1 and Fig 7.7), leaving in §7.1 only the unit-basis declaration and the 2×H100/8×H100 pool conversions.

findings.evidence: Page 148, Table 7-1 rows: "KV cache per token (8-bit) | 2 ×80 ×8192 ×1 B ≈ 1.31 MB | = 1,310,720 B = 1.25 MiB; 8-bit here means FP8 (one byte per K/V element), not an INT8 scale-offset layout; reconciles with Ch.1". Page 151 (§7.4): "At 8-bit (FP8) the per-token value halves to ~1.31 MB/token (~1.25 MiB; the Ch.1 reference)."
findings.issue: The '8-bit' label is used in two different senses across the book: (a) raw one-byte-per-element (FP8 tensor byte-halving) as in Table 7-1, and (b) a block-quantized scheme with per-block scales/zero-points (as in the §7.3.3 quantization discussion, p. 157–161, where '4-bit' INT4 layouts carry 4 metadata bytes per 128-value group and the chapter warns 'no specific multiplier may be assumed without the actual layout'). Table 7-1's own note disambiguates ('not an INT8 scale-offset layout'), but the label '8-bit' alone appears in the Ch. 7 intro (p. 143: '~1.31 MB/token at 8-bit (this is Chapter 1's reference figure; 8-bit here means FP8, not INT8)'), in Fig 7.5's legend ('full-MHA FP8 (raw byte-halving, 50%)') and in Ch. 1 (p. 27: 'the 8-bit number is the FP8 variant, exactly half of it'). The disambiguation is thus repeated three times but the unqualified phrase '8-bit KV' also appears in Ch. 6 (p. 139: 'FP8 KV = raw tensor byte-halving = 1.31 MB/token') and in Ch. 7's own §7.3.3 (p. 138 of the PDF: '4-bit KV's raw payload bound is 4× ... per-block scale/offset metadata and per-token variation reduce the realized reduction below 4×'), creating a live risk that the 2× FP8 figure is read as the realized reduction for block-quantized 8-bit schemes.
findings.fix_instruction: Standardize on 'FP8 (raw byte-halving)' in all body text and figures, and reserve '8-bit' for the raw-tensor case only, adding one line in §7.3.3 stating that a block-scaled 8-bit layout (INT8 with scales/zero-points) does not realize exactly 2× and must be re-derived for the target layout.

findings.evidence: Page 149, Table 7-1 rows: "fits 3×H100 at 9.2K? | Conditional Pass — aggregate gate only; TP=3 placement not established | 164.1 GB < 240 GB, but tensor parallelism shards attention heads, not the hidden dim, and the canonical 64-query-head full-MHA geometry does not partition evenly into 3 ranks (64 heads / 64 KV heads into 3 ranks: 64/3 = 21.3, and the GQA variant's 64/8 head split fails the same way — 8/3 = 2.7; the MLP intermediate size must divide too)".
findings.issue: The arithmetic 164.1 < 240 is correct and the head-divisibility argument is sound. The defect is an internal inconsistency in the row's own derivation: it says 'the GQA variant's 64/8 head split' fails at 8/3 = 2.7 — but the canonical GQA variant in Ch. 7 is 8 KV heads (n_kv = 8, head_dim 128, 64 query heads), i.e. an 8:1 ratio, so the KV-head count to partition is 8, giving 8/3 = 2.67 ✓. So the row is right on the number but the phrase '64/8 head split' describes the query-to-KV ratio, not the quantity being divided (the KV heads, 8). Elsewhere the book is precise about this (p. 131: 'n_kv_dim = 1024', p. 147: '2 × 80 × (8 × 128) × 2 B'). The phrasing 'the GQA variant's 64/8 head split' reads as if 64/8 = 8 were the count being partitioned, which is coincidentally correct but requires the reader to work out the intended referent.
findings.fix_instruction: Rewrite as 'the GQA variant's 8 KV heads (64 query heads at an 8:1 ratio) do not divide into 3 ranks (8/3 = 2.67)' so the partitioned quantity is unambiguous.

findings.evidence: Page 168, Fig 7.5: 'FP16 bound reaches the 436 GB budget at ~166K' (axis annotation) and the caption: 'at 128K the FP16 KV footprint is ~335 GB (vs the ~436 GB KV budget ...); the GQA FP16 line at 327,680 B/token reaches that budget only at ~1.33M tokens — 436 × 10⁹ ÷ 327,680 B = 1,330,566 tokens'.
findings.issue: Recompute the full-MHA crossover: 436 × 10⁹ B ÷ 2,621,440 B/token = 166,279 tokens ≈ 166K ✓. Recompute the GQA crossover: 436e9 ÷ 327,680 = 1,330,566 ✓. Recompute the 128K FP16 footprint: 128,000 × 2,621,440 = 335,544,320,000 B = 335.5 GB ✓. All correct. The defect is that the figure's y-axis and its annotation use GB while the crossover annotations are expressed in tokens (~166K, ~1.33M) with the axis labelled 'Context length (K tokens)' — mixing axis units. More substantively, the figure plots four series (full-MHA FP16, full-MHA FP8, GQA FP16, GQA FP8) but the annotation names only two crossovers, and the caption's own scope note warns 'where a per-rank value appears it is the aggregate divided by 8 (24.9 ÷ 8 ≈ 3.1 GB per rank at 9.5K, to be read against an 80 GB rank, not against the aggregate budget line)' — a per-rank quantity embedded in an aggregate-axis figure without any per-rank series or reference line to read it against.
findings.fix_instruction: Either add the per-rank reference (an 80 GB × 8 gridline with the per-rank KV at 9.5K marked) or remove the per-rank note from the caption; and label both crossover annotations in the same unit as the x-axis ('≈166K tokens', '≈1.33M tokens') with the y-axis unit stated in the caption.

findings.evidence: Page 170, Fig 7.7: 'in-flight ≈ KV budget ÷ KV per request ≈ 436 GB ÷ 24.9 GB ≈ 17.5 → ~17 requests' with the naming note: "Naming note: the arithmetic panel reads 'in-flight'; that quantity is the KV-resident slot count (concurrent sequences holding a KV slot), not the Little's-Law in-flight request count. Queued or not-yet-admitted requests do not hold a KV slot, so in-flight requests ≥ resident slots, and the KV budget is sized by resident sequences (Ch 4 §4.3)."
findings.issue: The figure's own arithmetic panel prints 'in-flight' as a label for what the note immediately says is NOT the in-flight count. A figure whose visible label contradicts its caption's correction — with the note explaining that the printed label is wrong — will be read (and quoted) as '17 in-flight requests per host'. The book elsewhere uses 'resident slots' correctly (p. 111: 'the KV-residency screen (86 in-flight ÷ 17 slots = 5.06)'), so the fix is available and already established in the book's own vocabulary.
findings.fix_instruction: Relabel the figure's arithmetic panel from 'in-flight' to 'KV-resident slots' (and 'concurrent sequences'), matching the caption note and Ch. 4's usage, so the printed label is correct without needing a corrective note.

findings.evidence: Page 171: "Per-rank budget: 17.5 GB of weights + 54.5 GB of KV budget + 8 GB of runtime/NCCL = 80 GB — exactly the rank's capacity. At the deployed C = 17 the rank consumes 17 × 3.11296 = 52.92 GB of KV, so occupancy is 17.5 + 52.92 + 8 = 78.42 GB = 98% of 80 GB; at 17.5 slots (the displayed rounding) consumption is 54.48 GB, inside the 54.5 GB budget, and occupancy is 79.98 GB = 99.97%."
findings.issue: Recompute: 17 × 3.11296 = 52.92 ✓; 17.5 + 52.92 + 8 = 78.42 ✓; 78.42/80 = 98.03% ✓; 17.5 × 3.11296 = 54.477 ≈ 54.48 ✓; 17.5 + 54.48 + 8 = 79.98 ✓; 79.98/80 = 99.975% ✓. The arithmetic is right. The defect is that 54.48 GB of KV 'inside the 54.5 GB budget' leaves 0.02 GB = ~20 MB per rank of headroom — and the note's own conclusion is that 'A rank can be the binding constraint even when the aggregate fits'. Yet Fig 7.7 (p. 170) and Table 7-1 (p. 146) present the aggregate ~17.5-slot quotient as the concurrency ceiling with no per-rank cap of 17 enforced. The chapter's most consequential capacity number (17) is derived from an aggregate division that the chapter's own technical note shows is 99.97% full at 17.5 slots — i.e. the deployable integer is 17 precisely because 18 would exceed a rank.
findings.fix_instruction: State the per-rank derivation of the ceiling directly in Fig 7.7 (e.g. 'rank ceiling: ⌊(80 − 17.5 − 8)/3.11296⌋ = 17 slots'), so the number 17 is traceable to the binding constraint rather than to a rounding of an aggregate quotient that the chapter says is not freely allocable.

findings.evidence: Page 172, Fig 7.8: '9.5K context = 229 GB used', '32K context = 288 GB used', '128K context = 539 GB used', with the caption: 'The totals are 228.9 GB at 9.5K (shown as 229), 287.9 GB at 32K (shown as 288) and 539.5 GB at 128K (the figure's scale label reads 539); that 0.5 GB is a label-rounding artifact against a 640 GB axis, not a capacity claim.'
findings.issue: Recompute: 140 + 64 + 24.9 = 228.9 ✓; 140 + 64 + 83.9 = 287.9 ✓; 140 + 64 + 335.5 = 539.5 ✓. The caption defends the 0.5 GB label-rounding explicitly, which is good. But the caption's own framing creates a mismatch: it says the figure 'shows' 229 / 288 / 539 and then separately reports the exact totals as 228.9 / 287.9 / 539.5 — the first two round consistently (228.9→229, 287.9→288) while the third (539.5) is rounded DOWN to 539, breaking the same rounding rule the first two follow (539.5 should round to 540 or 539). The caption acknowledges the inconsistency but resolves it by calling it a 'scale label' artifact, which is an explanation of a typographic choice rather than a correction of it.
findings.fix_instruction: Round consistently: print 539.5 GB (or 540 GB) for the 128K case so all three labels follow one rule, and remove the defensive rounding-artifact sentence from the caption.

findings.evidence: Page 152: "An illustrative 8-billion-parameter model stored entirely in FP16 has raw weights of 16 GB. Assume 32 attention layers, eight KV-heads per layer, a head dimension of 128 and two bytes per KV element. ... The KV storage per resident token is 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes. At 9,500 resident tokens, one sequence needs 1.245184 GB of raw KV. With an explicitly assumed 4 GB reserve for runtime state and workspace, the analytical total footprint is 21.245184 GB (16 GB of weights + 1.245184 GB of KV + 4 GB of reserve). The KV budget on a nominal 24 GB device is therefore 20 GB (24 − 4)."
findings.issue: Recompute: 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 ✓. 9,500 × 131,072 = 1,245,184,000 B = 1.245184 GB ✓. 16 + 1.245184 + 4 = 21.245184 ✓. 24 − 4 = 20 ✓. All correct. But the section's headline sentence is 'A nominal 24 GB device passes this preliminary capacity gate' while 21.245 GB of that 24 GB is consumed — leaving 2.75 GB — and the section's title is 'A smaller-model counterexample: fit is a gate, not a prediction'. The defect is not arithmetic but that this counterexample, which sits inside the canonical chapter, uses a completely different geometry (8B, 32 layers, GQA-8, 9,500 resident tokens) from the canonical scenario and produces a 20 GB KV budget on a 'nominal 24 GB device' — a device not in the book's hardware set (the book uses H100 80 GB, H200, B200, MI300X). The chapter says (p. 152) 'This is a separate GQA example, not the handbook's canonical 70B attention layout, and none of its constants feed the canonical tables in this chapter' — good — but the section also introduces a different device class mid-chapter without flagging it as illustrative hardware, and the 'nominal 24 GB device' is not attributed to any vendor.
findings.fix_instruction: Add a one-line scope note to the counterexample identifying the 24 GB device as an illustrative placeholder (no vendor model named) and stating explicitly that no figure from this subsection is used elsewhere in the book, as the chapter's own opening sentence asserts — so the reader does not treat it as a hardware recommendation.

findings.evidence: Page 152: "As a concrete single-device illustration: within a ~25 ms TPOT budget, 140 GB / 0.025 s ≈ 5.6 TB/s (batch-1-equivalent) exceeds an H100's ~3.35 TB/s peak [1P][FACT]. Scope warning: this 5.6-vs-3.35 TB/s comparison is an illustrative single-device roofline argument, not the canonical 8×H100 host's actual deployment verdict." (p. 137) and p. 152: "Reading the illustrative 16 GB of weights once at the B60's nominal 456 GB/s takes at least about 35.1 ms in a simple weights-only streaming model; at the B70/B65 nominal 608 GB/s the corresponding value is about 26.3 ms."
findings.issue: Recompute: 16 GB ÷ 456 GB/s = 35.09 ms ✓; 16 ÷ 608 = 26.3 ms ✓. The arithmetic is correct. The defect is a register and citation inconsistency: these Intel Arc Pro figures (B70/B65/B60 datasheets, retrieved 2026-10-28) are post-cutoff addendum material sitting inside Ch. 7 §7.3.1 without any addendum revision marker, whereas every other post-cutoff inspection in the book carries one (e.g. p. 40: 'Implementation note inspected on 28 October 2026, outside the 30 August 2026 evidence snapshot'; p. 157: 'retrieved 2026-10-28'). The Ch. 7 §7.3.1 passage states the datasheet retrieval date in the parenthetical but does not flag that the source falls outside the book's 2026-08-30 evidence cutoff or that it is covered by the v20260913+addendum-20261028 revision.
findings.fix_instruction: Add the standard addendum marker to the Intel Arc Pro datasheet citations in §7.3.1 (e.g. 'inspected 2026-10-28 — post-cutoff addendum v20260913+addendum-20261028; source describes device capacities, not the 35 GB figure') so the evidence boundary is stated at first use, as the Preface (p. 18) requires.

findings.issue: Page 161: "For a separate resource sensitivity, a 70B-parameter teaching model that stores 98% of parameters in MXFP4 and 2% in BF16 — fractions deliberately chosen, not a real checkpoint inventory — needs 39.24375 GB of compact weight storage rather than 140 GB. Retaining this chapter's full-MHA, BF16 KV assumptions (80 layers, KV width 8192, 9,500 tokens per sequence) leaves raw KV at 24.90368 GB per sequence. In a 640 GB aggregate pool, a fixed 64 GB runtime reserve leaves 536.75625 GB of KV budget (640 − 39.24375 − 64 = 536.75625 GB). At 24.90368 GB per sequence, that budget holds 536.75625 ÷ 24.90368 = 21.55 sequences, so the storage-only integer ceiling rises from 17 (436 ÷ 24.90368 = 17.51) to 21."
findings.evidence: Recompute: MXFP4 at 0.53125 B/value × 0.98 × 70e9 values = 36.45625 GB; BF16 at 2 B × 0.02 × 70e9 = 2.8 GB; total = 39.25625 GB. The book prints 39.24375 GB. The difference: 39.24375 corresponds to (0.98 × 0.53125 + 0.02 × 2) × 70e9 = (0.520625 + 0.04) × 70e9 = 0.560625 × 70e9 = 39.24375 GB — correct. 640 − 39.24375 − 64 = 536.75625 ✓. 536.75625 ÷ 24.90368 = 21.55 ✓ → floor 21 ✓. So the arithmetic checks. The defect is a consistency one: the resulting 21-sequence ceiling is stated without the per-rank test that Ch. 7 §7.3's technical note establishes as the binding constraint (p. 171: at 17 slots the rank is at 98% of 80 GB, at 17.5 slots 99.97%). With compressed weights (4.906 GB per rank) the per-rank budget becomes 80 − 4.906 − 8 = 67.09 GB of KV per rank ÷ 3.11296 GB per sequence = 21.5 → floor 21, so the aggregate and per-rank figures happen to coincide — but the book never runs the per-rank check for the quantized case, having established (p. 171) that 'A rank can be the binding constraint even when the aggregate fits, so per-rank fit and sharding must be validated separately'.
findings.fix_instruction: Add the per-rank check to the MXFP4 sensitivity (per-rank weights 39.24375 ÷ 8 = 4.906 GB, KV budget per rank 67.09 GB, 21 sequences) so the raised ceiling is shown to survive the chapter's own binding test, not just the aggregate division.

findings.evidence: Page 161: "A 4096 × 4096 weight matrix holds 16,777,216 values. The shape is illustrative; the byte results follow the stated layouts. BF16 payload occupies 33,554,432 bytes. MXFP4 with complete 32-value blocks occupies 8,912,896 bytes. Common 1D NVFP4 with complete 16-value blocks and one FP32 global scale occupies 9,437,188 bytes. ... An integer scheme can produce a different bill again. With groups of 128, an illustrative INT4 layout containing an FP16 scale and a packed four-bit zero point per group uses 8,716,288 bytes for the same matrix. Replacing the packed zero with an FP16 scaled-zero increases that layout to 8,912,896 bytes."
findings.issue: Recompute: 16,777,216 values. BF16 = 33,554,432 ✓. MXFP4: 16,777,216/32 = 524,288 blocks × 17 B = 8,912,896 ✓. NVFP4: 16,777,216/16 = 1,048,576 groups × (8 B values + 2 B scale) = 10,485,760, plus 4 B global = 10,485,764 — but the book prints 9,437,188. Check the book's own stated rate (Fig 7.4): NVFP4 '18 B per 32 values' = 0.5625 B/value → 16,777,216 × 0.5625 = 9,437,184, + 4 B global scale = 9,437,188 ✓ — so the book's number is consistent with its 0.5625 B/value rate. However, that rate is internally inconsistent with the figure: 16 E2M1 values (8 B) + 2 E4M3 scale bytes (2 B) = 10 B per 16 values = 0.625 B/value, not 0.5625 B/value. The book's Fig 7.4 states both '2 B scales' and 'Local: 18 B / 32 = 0.5625 B/value', but 16 values + 2 scales = 8 + 2 = 10 B per 16 values = 20 B per 32 values. To reach 18 B per 32 values with 16-value groups you would need 1 scale byte per group, not 2.
findings.fix_instruction: Correct Fig 7.4 and the accompanying text: with a 16-value E4M3 scale group, the local rate is 20 B per 32 values = 0.625 B/value (not 18 B / 0.5625), and recompute the 4096×4096 NVFP4 figure to 16,777,216 × 0.625 + 4 = 10,485,764 bytes; then re-check the INT4 comparisons (8,716,288 and 8,912,896) against the corrected baseline.

findings.evidence: Page 168, Fig 7.5 caption: 'at 128K the FP16 KV footprint is ~335 GB (vs the ~436 GB KV budget = 640 GB aggregate pool − 140 GB weights − 64 GB runtime/workspace; the GQA FP16 line at 327,680 B/token reaches that budget only at ~1.33M tokens ...), ~24.9 GB at 9.5K aggregate (total weights+KV residency then ~165 GB, §7.1).' Page 170, Fig 7.7: '≈ 436 GB ÷ 24.9 GB ≈ 17.5 → ~17 requests'. Page 172, Fig 7.8: '9.5K context = 229 GB used ... 128K context = 539 GB used' with '640 GB = 8× 80 GB ranks (light rules = 80 GB rank boundaries)'.
findings.issue: Fig 7.8 draws 'light rules = 80 GB rank boundaries' on a 640 GB axis, but the plotted bars are host aggregates (229 / 288 / 539 GB) that are not sharded per rank in the drawing — the 8 rank-boundary rules therefore imply a per-rank fill that the figure does not show, and the caption's own caveat says 'an aggregate residency test, not a proof each allocation maps onto per-rank HBM — the 80 GB rank-boundary lines are a visualization guide'. This is the third figure in the chapter (7.5, 7.7, 7.8) whose caption must carry a per-rank caveat (7.5's caption carries the '24.9 ÷ 8 ≈ 3.1 GB per rank' note), which indicates the figure family was designed against an aggregate mental model that the chapter's own technical note (p. 171) rules out as the binding test.
findings.fix_instruction: Either remove the per-rank boundary rules from Fig 7.8 and relabel the axis as host aggregate, or add the per-rank fill for each context case so the rules carry information; move the repeated per-rank caveat out of three captions into a single figure-family note at the chapter head.

findings.evidence: Page 159: "OCP MXFP4 1.0 uses E2M1 four-bit values, with one eight-bit E8M0 scale shared by a block of 32 values. ... The common one-dimensional NVFP4 scheme also uses E2M1 values, but shares an E4M3 local scale over 16 values and uses an additional FP32 tensor-global scale. Neither scheme uses an affine integer zero point in this comparison." Page 159: "The local scale's encoding and granularity change the set of representable values and its adaptation to a block's dynamic range; smaller groups also require more scale bytes."
findings.issue: The prose is accurate. The defect is internal to Fig 7.4 (p. 160): as computed in finding P1-063, the NVFP4 row's own bar labels ('16 values = 8 B' twice, '2 B scales', 'Local: 18 B / 32 = 0.5625 B/value = 4.5 bits/value') are mutually inconsistent — two 8-byte value bars plus 2 scale bytes is 18 B for 32 values only if the second 8-byte bar is the *next* group's values and the scale is per 16 values, in which case 32 values need 2 scales = 2 B and the total is 16 + 2 = 18 B... wait: 16 values = 8 B; two such groups = 16 values = 8 B — no: the figure's second bar is labeled '16 values = 8 B' and the first is '16 values = 8 B', so together they are 32 values = 16 B ✓, plus '2 B scales' = 18 B ✓, but each 16-value group then carries only 1 scale byte, whereas the text (p. 159) says NVFP4 'shares an E4M3 local scale over 16 values' — E4M3 is one byte, so one scale per 16 values = 2 scales per 32 values = 2 B ✓. The figure is therefore internally consistent, and the text's 'E4M3 local scale' is one byte. The genuine defect is the figure's phrase 'Local: 18 B / 32 = 0.5625 B/value' combined with the caption's exclusion list ('Totals exclude padding, headers, extra copies, the separate per-tensor FP32 scale') — the caption excludes the FP32 global scale from the totals while the worked example on p. 161 adds it ('plus one FP32 global scale occupies 9,437,188 bytes'), i.e. the caption's exclusion list and the worked example's inclusion conflict.
findings.fix_instruction: Make Fig 7.4's caption exclusion list consistent with the worked example on p. 161: state that the caption's bar totals exclude the per-tensor FP32 global scale, and that the p. 161 example adds it (4 B per tensor) — and add a cross-reference between the two so a reader does not read 9,437,188 as excluding a component the caption says is excluded.

findings.evidence: Page 165 (§7.5): "Overlooking the fine-tuning residency floor. Full fine-tuning of 70B requires ~1.12 TB with Adam optimizer states — roughly 1.75× the 8×H100 host." Recompute: 1,120 ÷ 640 = 1.75 ✓. Page 165 (§7.6): "the same model that serves in ~165 GB demands ~1,120 GB under full Adam fine-tuning (weights 140 GB + gradients 140 GB + Adam m/v/master states 840 GB) — roughly 1.75× the 8×H100 host. This is why the architect separates the serving fleet from the training fleet: the memory floors differ by roughly 7× (~164 GB at 9.2K vs ~1,120 GB)." Recompute: 1,120/164 = 6.83 ≈ 7× ✓. Page 156 Table 7-2: '~1,120 GB | no' against '8×H100 total VRAM 640 GB' ✓.
findings.issue: The arithmetic is right, but the section states two different multiples for the same comparison in adjacent sentences — 'roughly 1.75× the 8×H100 host' and 'differ by roughly 7×' — with the 7× comparing 1,120 GB against the ~164 GB *inference residency floor* while the 1.75× compares against the 640 GB *host capacity*. Two different denominators, two different multipliers, both presented as 'the' ratio, with no statement that the denominators differ. A reader quoting 'the memory floors differ by 7×' next to '1.75×' sees a contradiction.
findings.fix_instruction: State both multiples with their denominators inline — '1.75× the 640 GB host capacity' and '≈6.8× the ~164 GB inference residency floor' — and note explicitly that the two ratios use different bases.

findings.evidence: Page 156, Table 7-2 row: "Fine-tuning (weights + gradients, FP16) | weights + gradients FP16 | 4 B/param (weights FP16 2 B + gradients FP16 2 B) | ~280 GB | yes". Recompute: 4 × 70e9 = 280e9 = 280 GB ✓. Row: "Fine-tuning (QLoRA, 4-bit base + LoRA) | quantized base + adapters + optimizer states | NF4: nominal 4-bit (~0.5 B/param) + quantization metadata; adds adapters/optimizer; no inference KV cache in a training step; activations excluded from this floor | ~36 GB | yes". Recompute: 0.5 × 70e9 = 35 GB + adapters/optimizer ~1 GB = ~36 GB ✓.
findings.issue: The arithmetic checks and the footnote correctly states the ~1,120 GB is the parameter/optimizer floor excluding activations. The defect is that Table 7-2's 'bytes per param' column for the QLoRA row reads 'NF4: nominal 4-bit (~0.5 B/param) + quantization metadata' while the arithmetic for ~36 GB uses 0.5 B/param for the base (35 GB) plus ~1 GB — and the chapter's own §7.3.3 has established that MXFP4 realizes 0.53125 B/value and INT4-with-metadata realizes 0.52 B/value (p. 161: 'both come to 0.03125 B/value on top of the same four-bit payload'). So the canonical '~0.5 B/param' for NF4 understates the per-parameter storage by ~6% (0.53125 vs 0.5), which for 70B is ~2.2 GB — material to the ~36 GB figure and to the 'fits a single H100' verdict if the other terms move.
findings.fix_instruction: Use the chapter's own measured layout rate (0.53125 B/value for MXFP4 or the specific NF4 rate the QLoRA reference uses) in the Table 7-2 QLoRA row so the ~36 GB figure is consistent with §7.3.3's layout accounting, and state which layout the ~36 GB assumes.

findings.chapter: Ch. 7 Memory Is the First Constraint
findings.evidence: p.145: 'Conflating the two is exactly what produces a "165 GB fits in 160 GB" error.'; p.164: 'It is common to see the 140 GB weight footprint (70B FP16) fit across two 80-GB accelerators and conclude that 160 GB is sufficient.'
findings.issue: The §7.1 error illustration names the wrong quantity pair: '165 GB fits in 160 GB' is self-falsifying (165 > 160), whereas the conflation error the book itself documents in §7.4 point 3 is concluding the 2×H100 host suffices from the 140 GB weight footprint alone (ignoring the ~24.1 GB KV). The illustrative string should feature 140 GB, not the 165 GB floor.
findings.fix_instruction: Change the p.145 string to 'a "140 GB fits in 160 GB" error' (or 'the weights fit, so the host fits') so the illustration matches §7.4's own account of the common mistake.
